newsitem.title: USA: Boeing, McDonnell chiefs see U.S. approving merger.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, McDonnell chiefs see U.S. approving merger.

text.p: The chief executive officers of Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp predicted Sunday that the companies' proposed merger into the world's largest aerospace concern would pass government scrutiny, but not immediately.

"I think there obviously will be questions," Phil Condit, president and chief executive officer of Boeing, told reporters at the news conference at which the $13.3 billion deal was announced. But he said he was confident the government would not stand in its way.

Condit estimated it would take six months for the two companies to complete their merger, allowing plenty of time for the government to review the military and civilian manufacturing capabilities of both.

Only last week, Boeing finished digesting the defense and aerospace units of Rockwell International Corp. in a $3.2 billion deal that took several months. The government found no anti-trust violations in that combination.
Condit said he was confident it would be unnecessary for the merged company, which will be called Boeing, to divest itself of any of its parts to comply with laws designed to preserve competition.
"We have looked very carefully at the programs. They are largely complementary," he told reporters.
Condit said that within the next two weeks, he and McDonnell Douglas President Harry Stonecipher would talk to the Department of Defense and file the necessary papers with the Justice Department.
The Pentagon must review the deal because, according to figures provided by Boeing, 75 percent of McDonnell Douglas' business and 40 percent of Boeing's is with the military.
"It will certainly reduce competition when it comes to bidding contracts for the military," said Lawrence Crawford of Reston, Virginia, consulting firm Avitas Aviation.
But when it comes to the commercial airline division of McDonnell Douglas, Crawford said: "This save's Douglas's life. Airbus has been taking market share out of Douglas daily."

Within the past month, McDonnell Douglas canceled development of a wide-bodied commercial airplane because of competition from Boeing and Airbus. Instead it announced a collaboration with Boeing to develop the successor to the Boeing 747.
Darrell Jenkins of the Consultancy Aviation Foundation in Falls Church, Virginia, said that without a full product line, Douglas was unable to compete.
Once the companies file papers at the Justice Department, a 30-day clock will start running, although it can be stopped and extended.
Robert Skitol, an antitrust attorney in Washington, said there would certainly be an "intense and thorough" antitrust investigation that would take far longer than 30 days.
Another anti-trust attorney with airline experience, Don Farmer of Washington, said, "The largest concern is that they are two of the three commercial airframe manufacturers in the world."
